data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a methodological commitment to 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) and the pragmatic necessity of acting on the most severely tested available option, while explicitly accepting that this preference carries no guarantee of truth or probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude itself requires inductive assumptions to link past testing to future truth-likeness, the defense collapses into the induction it seeks to avoid.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's rejection of evolutionary epistemology removes the biological/pragmatic basis for preferring tested theories, the 'necessity' of choice becomes arbitrary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the distinction between 'acting on' and 'believing in' a theory is merely semantic when the outcome of action depends on the theory's truth, the smuggling of induction is confirmed.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument distinguishes between 'epistemic probability' (which Popper rejects as unattainable via induction) and 'methodological rationality' (which demands choosing the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification). The mechanism relies on the concept of verisimilitude: while we cannot know a theory is true, a highly corroborated theory is logically closer to the truth than a falsified one or an untested one, provided it has higher empirical content. The preference is a rule of action ('act on the best-tested') rather than a belief state ('expect this to work').","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
